title: Section 151 — Assaulting President, Governor, etc. with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power

content.overview: BNS s. 151 — Assaulting President, Governor, etc. with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Assaulting President, Governor, etc. with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power. Historical concordance: IPC 124. For conduct governed by the BNS, cite BNS section 151; the IPC reference is historical concordance.
In student language: BNS s. 151 is the rule on “Assaulting President, Governor, etc. with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power”. The section provides that whoever, with the intention of inducing or compelling the President of India, or Governor of any State, to exercise or refrain from exercising in any manner any of the lawful powers of such President or Governor, assaults or wrongfully restrains, or attempts wrongfully to restrain, or overawes, by means of criminal force or the show of criminal force, or attempts so to overawe, such President or Governor, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 151 exists so that “Assaulting President, Governor, etc. with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power” has a closed legal test in Chapter VII — Of Offences Against the State. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Waging war, and the new s. 152 on sovereignty, unity and integrity — not a relabel of sedition.

The provision in detail
151. Whoever, with the intention of inducing or compelling the President of India, or Governor of any State, to exercise or refrain from exercising in any manner any of the lawful powers of such President or Governor, assaults or wrongfully restrains, or attempts wrongfully to restrain, or overawes, by means of criminal force or the show of criminal force, or attempts so to overawe, such President or Governor, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine

Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:

essentialIngredients: The commission of an act or omission falling within the statutory description of Assaulting President, Governor, etc. with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power.
The existence of the requisite culpable mental state (intention, knowledge, rashness, or negligence) prescribed under Section 151.

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 151 constitutes a key component of Chapter VII (Of Offences against the State) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, addressing assaulting president, governor, etc. with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power. The provision balances personal liberty with public interest and social order. The prosecution must establish every statutory element beyond reasonable doubt: the specified actus reus, the requisite mens rea, and any relevant statutory circumstances. Modern judicial interpretation emphasizes substantive fairness, proportionality in sentencing, and adherence to constitutional safeguards. Where statutory exceptions or provisos are attached to the section, the accused must establish facts bringing the case within such provisions under evidentiary standards.
examples: Teaching example (Standard application): An individual intentionally commits acts satisfying the statutory formula of assaulting president, governor, etc. with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power under Section 151 without lawful authority. The individual is liable under BNS s. 151.

Teaching example (Absence of mens rea / Lawful exception): A person acts in good faith or without the requisite statutory mental element under circumstances recognized by law. The essential ingredients of Section 151 are not satisfied; no penal liability attaches.
distinctions: Section 151 vs General Attempt: Section 151 penalizes the substantive conduct specified in Chapter VII; inchoate attempts without specific provisions fall under the general attempt provisions.
Section 151 vs Cognate Chapter Offences: Liability under Section 151 is distinguished by its specific mental threshold and the particular legal interest protected under Of Offences against the State.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether the accused is liable under BNS s. 151 for conduct relating to assaulting president, governor, etc. with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power.
Rule: Under BNS s. 151, liability attaches upon proof of the statutory actus reus accompanied by the requisite mens rea without lawful justification.
Application: The evidence demonstrates that the accused performed the specified act with the required state of mind, satisfying all statutory ingredients of Section 151.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of an offence under BNS s. 151 and subject to the prescribed punishment.
